newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ministers back Airbus in U.S. row.
newsitem.headline: Ministers back Airbus in U.S. row.

text.p: European ministers on Monday threw their support behind partners in the four-nation Airbus consortium who fear a U.S. mega-merger, and backed moves to change the partnership into a limited company.
Ministers were meeting at the Paris air show where Airbus Industrie and arch rival Boeing Co have been fighting a running battle over Boeing's proposed takeover of McDonnell Douglas.

The British, French, German and Spanish ministers, after meeting the Airbus partners on Monday at the air show, said they wanted the United States to observe a 1992 aviation trade pact on subsidies but stopped short of calling for a renegotiation.

Airbus partners say Boeing-McDonnell Douglas will dominate the market by its sheer size -- with combined sales in aerospace and defence totalling $48 billion, and would increase the potential for hefty U.S. military spending to cross-subsidise the commercial aircraft business.

German Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt said the merger "will create a unique technology competence that gives Boeing the possibility to further expand its market position through strengthened cross-subsidies between the civil and military sectors".
France's newly-appointed commmunist transport minister Jean-Claude Gayssot added his voice to the concerns, "We have decided not to accept this unfair competition".

Controversial exclusive supply agreements between Boeing and major U.S. airlines AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental and Delta Air Lines have also angered Airbus as well as the European Commission, which is investigating the U.S. merger on competition grounds.
" The deals commit the airlines to buying only Boeing jets. Boeing said this week that the deals were done at the behest of the airlines which were already Boeing customers.

Boeing is hoping for a ruling on the merger from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission by early July, which could leave Europe at odds with Washington if the European Commission were to rule against the deal and raise the prospect of a trade war.

But Britain's trade and industry minister Margaret Beckett said "there is no question of anyone seeking a trade war." Trade should be made as transparent as possible and the 1992 agreement should be "applied scrupulously," she told a news conference.

But behind the scenes of ministerial solidarity, a row was still raging between the French state-owned partner, Aerospatiale, and major partners British Aerospace Plc (BAe) and Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa). Spain's Casa is the fourth Airbus partner.

A BAe official told Reuters BAe and Dasa had written to Aerospatiale to spell out their insistence that the future Airbus will own and control its design offices and factories, to make it more competitive and confront a strengthened Boeing.
"It's a question of making one's point very clear," the BAe official told Reuters.

Aerospatiale chairman Yves Michot told journalists before the air show the partners had all agreed the new Airbus would have only a "management mandate" and assets would remain in the partner firms. That was seen by analysts as Aerospatiale's way of hanging onto its crown jewels, its design office.
But BAe and Dasa, not content with putting their views in writing, sent copies of the letters to the French transport minister, which was seen here as a rebuke to Aerospatiale.

Britain's Beckett lent her support to BAe and Dasa in a statement issued on Monday, reminding Aerospatiale that the four Airbus partners signed a memorandum of understanding in January, which agreed that they would pool their Airbus assets.

"The consortium signed a memorandum of understanding in January 1997 outlining the terms of the eventual SCE (single corporate entity) and targets relating to achieving this goal. This involves the pooling of core resources such as design, engineering, procurement and assembly in order to help maintain Airbus's competitiveness in global markets.
"The four ministers welcomed this objective and shared the determination of the industry to reach a satisfactory agreement within the lines and times laid down in the MOU signed in January.
